lesson.title: Copied but Still Connected: Understanding Shallow Copy
lesson.summary: A shallow copy, made with copy(), list(), or slicing, duplicates the outer list but not the objects nested inside it, so nested lists remain shared between the original and the copy.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed that original.copy() gives you a genuinely separate list from original, so appending to one no longer affects the other. That is entirely true, but it comes with a limit that only shows up once a list contains other lists. copy(), along with list() and slicing with [:], all perform what is called a shallow copy: they build a new outer list, but for each element that is itself a mutable object, like a nested list, the copy stores a reference to that exact same inner object rather than a fresh copy of it. The outer container is new, the things inside it are not.

```python
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = matrix.copy()
shallow[0][0] = 99
print(matrix)
print(shallow)
```

This prints:

```
[[99, 2], [3, 4]]
[[99, 2], [3, 4]]
```

matrix.copy() did create a new outer list for shallow, which is why shallow and matrix are not the same list object. But shallow[0] and matrix[0] are still the same inner list object, the one holding [1, 2]. When shallow[0][0] = 99 reaches into that shared inner list and changes it, the change is visible through matrix too, because there was never a second copy of that inner list to begin with, only a second reference to the original one.

It helps to contrast that with what happens if you replace an entire inner list rather than editing inside it:

```python
shallow[1] = [50, 60]
print(matrix)
print(shallow)
```

This prints:

```
[[99, 2], [3, 4]]
[[99, 2], [50, 60]]
```

This time matrix does not change. shallow[1] = [50, 60] does not reach into the old inner list and edit it, it points shallow's slot at index 1 to a brand new list object entirely, leaving matrix[1] pointing at the original [3, 4] it always had. The pattern to hold onto is this: mutating a shared inner object through either name affects both, because there is only one such object, but reassigning a slot to a new object only affects the name you reassigned through. Shallow copy protects the outer list, and nothing deeper than that. When you truly need every level of a nested list to be independent, you need the tool covered next, a deep copy.
